Definition and etiology

0:30 in the video

Inflammation of pancreas caused by activation of pancreatic enzymes => autodigestion

Overstimulation of pancreas: in alcoholic patients, and high dietary fat

Duct obstruction: obstruction of pancreatic duct => interstitial edema, impaired blood flow and acinar injury => activation of enzymes and autodigestion

Gallstones; Sickle cell disease, Cystic fibrosis (inherited); Choledochal cysts, Pancreas divisum (congenital)

Direct acinar cells injury: releases of proenzymes and further injury and activation of enzymes => autodigestion

Alcohol, drugs (Azathioprine, hydrochlorothiazide, Pentamidine); Trauma; Ischemia; Hypertriglyceridemia, Hypercalcemia, hyperthyroidism; infections

Defective intracellular transport: intracellular activation of enzymes => acinar cell injury => autodigestion

Alcohol; Duct obstruction

Severe acute pancreatitis

3:00 in the video

In severe acute pancreatitis, there is release of cytokines, toxic enzymes, and mediators into the circulation and activation of systemic inflammatory response, and this leads to:

Leukocytosis; DIC; ARDS; Hemolysis; Peripheral vascular collapse; Shock

Medical emergency

Patient presentation — history

3:50 in the video

Severe epigastric pain with radiation to the back, aggravated by meals

Nausea

Vomiting

Anorexia

Low grade fever

Patient presentation — examination

4:30 in the video

Epigastric tenderness

Abdominal distension (epigastric region)

Palpable abdominal mass (if pseudocyst developed)

Decreased bowel sounds

Jaundice

Tachycardia => because of pain, dehydration

Hypotension => dehydration, sepsis because of infection

Cullen’s sign => discoloration of the periumbilical region

Grey Turner’s sign => discoloration of the flanks

Diagnosis

5:50 in the video

Labs: Serum lipase more specific than amylase, and it is elevated within 4 to 8 hours, peaks in 24 hours and remain elevated for 1 to 2 weeks

LFT: if elevated => gallstone pancreatitis, RFT

Blood glucose, Ca level, CBC, lipid profile, serum LDH

CRP

Imaging: AXR/CXR: pleural effusion, ARDS

CT: useful for complications

ERCP: reserved for therapeutic interventions

MRCP: diagnostic use

Ranson’s criteria

8:40 in the video

Predict the prognosis of acute pancreatitis

At admission: Age > 55 years; WBC > 16000 cell/mm3; Glucose > 200 mg/dl; LDH > 350 IU/L; AST > 250 U/L

During 48 hours: Hematocrit fall > 10%; BUN rise > 5 mg/dl; PaO2 < 60 mmHg; Base deficit > 5 mEq/L; Serum calcium < 2 mmol/L; Fluid sequestration > 6 L

Interpretation

10:30 in the video

Ranson score of 3 or more indicate severe acute pancreatitis

Ranson score also predict mortality

Less than 3: Less than 1%

3–4: 15%

5–6: 40%

More than 6: 100%

Treatment

11:10 in the video

Bowel rest (NPO) and restart feeding after resolution but if there is severe inflammation then inducing early enteral feeding is important

IVF, ringer lactate is preferred unless hypercalcemia is the cause of acute pancreatitis, first 24h from 2500–4000ml total, and then accordingly

Analgesia: acetaminophen if mild pain, tramadol, meperidine

Antibiotics: cover enteric anaerobic and aerobic microorganisms, imipenem, ampicillin, ceftriaxone

ERCP for gallstone pancreatitis

Drainage of infected pancreatic collections

Surgical: necrosectomy

Complications

14:00 in the video

Local: Necrosis => inflammation; Pseudocysts, Pancreatic abscess => disruption of the pancreatic duct

Systemic: ARDS => microthrombi in the pulmonary vessels; Hypocalcemia => sequestration of calcium in fat necrosis; Hyperglycemia => disruption of islets of Langerhans; Shock and dehydration; DIC

GIT complications: GIT bleeding => gastric or duodenal erosions from pancreatic enzymes; Jaundice => compression by pseudocyst or gallstones pancreatitis
